abstract: |
  This report investigates the association between survey mode and undecided voter in 2012 and 2016 US state level election polls with consideration to the number of days unill the election. Using polling data from HuffPost Pollster/rOpenGov and official electoral results from MIT Election Data and Science Lab, the analysis evaluates 1219 polls from a 90 period prior to the elections. The absolute polling error was calculated by taking the Democrat-Republican polling margin and comparing it to the actual margin from the election results. Multiple linear regression models were created to find any associations between polling error, polling method and undecided voter share and any differences over the two election periods. The results indicated that there were small associations between the predictors and response, but no singular predictor was statistically significant. In all, it was found that there is no significant evidece undecided voter share and polling method alone are associated with differences in polling accuracy suggesting that other factors may influence polling error.

```{r}

library(tidyverse)

# Load the final analysis dataset
```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Pre-electoral polling plays an important role in understanding the public's political opinions and stances during election periods and can assist in predicting the outcomes of elections [@traugott_2005]. Polling on a state level is particularly insightful in the United States, as the results are determined by the Electoral College as opposed to national popular vote or preferential voting [@soumbatiants_chappell_johnson_2006]. Relative support for candidates on a state level can be estimated through polls, which can help assess how competitive each individual electoral contest is [@soumbatiants_chappell_johnson_2006]. While polling is an insightful tool, it does not always accurately reflect the final results of elections [@traugott_2005]. This is why it is important to understand what factors are associated with discrepancies between actual voting outcomes and polling estimates.

This analysis focuses on two polling features that may be associated with polling error: the proportion of undecided voters and the survey mode used to obtain responses. Only polls within 90 days of the elections will be considered. The number of undecided voters may increase uncertainty as to which party/candidate is more likely to win prior to the election. Similarly, certain survey modes may collect more accurate polling data than others. Through examining these variables, it may become evident that certain poll types will predict outcomes that are close to actual election results. Comparing 2012 and 2016 election polls and results allows the investigation of whether associations between polling error and polling characteristics are consistent across election periods. This analysis investigates how survey mode and reported undecided voter share are associated with state-level polling error, after accounting for time before Election Day, and whether these associations differ between the 2012 and 2016 elections.

# Method {#sec-method}

## Data

This study used three datasets: state-level presidential polling data from the 2012 and 2016 U.S. elections, obtained through the HuffPost Pollster/rOpenGov collection, and presidential election results from the MIT Election Data and Science Lab (MEDSL). The polling datasets contained 1,135 records from 2012 and 1,303 from 2016, including polling dates, states, survey modes, candidate support percentages, undecided voter share and sample sizes. Each polling record was treated as one observation. 

The election results were restricted to 2012 and 2016 and used to calculate actual state-level Democratic–Republican vote margins.

The variables used in the final analysis are summarised in @tbl-descriptives.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-descriptives
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of numerical variables in the final analysis sample."

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

analysis_data <- read_csv(
  "project datasets/analysis_data_final.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

analysis_data |>
  select(absolute_error, Undecided, days_to_election) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) |>
  group_by(Variable) |>
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD = sd(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  kable(digits = 2, col.names = c("Variable", "Mean", "SD"))
```

## Data Preparation and Sample Selection

The 2012 and 2016 polling datasets were combined after standardising state names, election years and polling dates to ensure consistency. The initial data cleaning was described in our EDA report. Official election results were then matched to the polling data by state and year. Before calculating actual election margins, votes received by the same major-party candidate under different party labels were combined to avoid underestimating their total support.

The analysis was restricted to polls ending within 90 days before Election Day. This period was selected to focus on polls conducted closer to the election. However, this restriction excludes earlier polls and limits the conclusions to the selected pre-election period. Records with missing or non-positive sample sizes, unavailable polling errors or missing undecided voter shares were excluded, leaving 1,561 observations at this stage. Missing undecided values were not replaced with zero because missing information does not necessarily indicate that no respondents were undecided.

The primary analysis focused on Live Phone, Internet and IVR/Online polls, reducing the sample to 1,221 observations. These three survey modes were selected because they were represented in both election years, allowing comparisons of their relationships with polling error. Other modes were excluded because they had limited representation or were not available consistently across both years. Consequently, the findings cannot be generalised to all survey modes.

Finally, two polls for which the sum of reported response percentages exceeded 102% were excluded from the main analysis, leaving 1,219 polls. The number of polls remaining after each selection step is shown in @tbl-sample-selection. As these totals do not necessarily indicate errors, both polls were included in a sensitivity analysis to assess whether their exclusion affected the results.

### Variable construction

Polling accuracy was measured using the absolute difference between the reported Democratic–Republican polling margin and the actual election margin.

The polling margin was calculated as:

$$
\text{Poll margin}
= \text{Democratic poll percentage} - \text{Republican poll percentage}
$$

The actual election margin was calculated as:

$$
\text{Actual margin}
= \frac{\text{Democratic votes} - \text{Republican votes}}
       {\text{Total votes}}
  \times 100
$$

Votes received by the same candidate under different party labels were combined before calculating the actual margin. Absolute polling error was then defined as:

$$
\text{Absolute error}
= \left| \text{Poll margin} - \text{Actual margin} \right|
$$

A lower absolute error indicates greater polling accuracy. All margins and errors were expressed in percentage points.

The main explanatory variables were reported undecided voter share and survey mode. Undecided voter share was measured as a percentage. Days before Election Day was calculated from each poll's end date, while election year distinguished the 2012 and 2016 observations. Survey mode and election year were treated as categorical variables.

## Statistical methods

In this report multiple linear regression was used to examine how polling error was associated with survey mode and the reported percentage of undecided voters, while accounting for the number of days before the election. It was also examined whether these associations differed between the 2012 and 2016 elections.

The response variable was the square root of absolute polling error. This transformation was chosen after comparing diagnostic plots for models using the original error, $\log(1 + \text{absolute error})$, and the square root of the error. The explanatory variables were election year, survey mode, undecided voter percentage and days before the election. Election year and survey mode were treated as categorical variables, with 2012 and Live Phone as the reference groups.

An additive model and an interaction model were fitted using the square-root-transformed response. The additive model assumed that the associations between the explanatory variables and polling error were the same in both years. The interaction model allowed the associations of survey mode, undecided voter percentage and days before the election with polling error to differ by year. The two nested models were compared using an F-test. The model comparison is provided in @tbl-app-model-comparison. The final model was selected by considering the research question, model comparison and diagnostic plots.

Residuals against fitted values and a Scale–Location plot were examined to assess the model form and the spread of residuals. A normal Q–Q plot was used to assess residual normality, and Cook’s distance was used to identify potentially influential observations. The diagnostic plots for the final model are shown in @fig-diagnostics. Code for the models using the original, log-transformed and square-root responses is available in `model_analysis.R` in the project repository.

A sensitivity analysis was conducted by refitting the final model after adding back the two polls with unusual reported response totals. The estimated coefficients were compared with and without these polls. The coefficient comparison is provided in @tbl-app-sensitivity. Because polls from the same state or pollster may not be independent, the usual confidence intervals and p-values are interpreted with caution.

# Results {#sec-results}

<!-- See rubric: Results - describe analysis w.r.t. the question; visualise; check assumptions. -->

Using linear regression the association of year, percentage of undecided voters from total voters polled, number of days to election, and mode of polling to the square root of the absolute error between pollster results and election results is best described by:

sqrt(absolute_error)=1.571+0.529×1\[year=2016\]+0.0273×\[Undecided\]+0.001×\[days_to_election\]-0.198×1\[mode=Internet\]-0.216×1\[mode=IVR/Online\]-0.0233×1\[year=2016\]×\[Undecided\]+0.001×1\[year=2016\]×\[days_to_election\]+0.376×1\[year=2016\]×1\[mode=Internet\]+0.0753×1\[year=2016\]×1\[mode=IVR/Online\]

year2016 and year2016:modeInternet coefficients are indicated as statistically significant with p values of 0.0000966 and 0.00256 respectively 

```{r}
#| label: conf-interval
#| tbl-cap: "Confidence intervals of model coefficients."
#confidence intervals for model coefficients 
confint(model_sqrt, level = 0.95)
```

```{r}
#| label: anova
#| tbl-cap: "Analysis of variance between additive and interaction models"
anova(model_sqrt_additive, model_sqrt)
```
comparison between additive and interaction models using analysis of variance table shows that F-test statistic is 3.068 with a P-value of 0.0158, which is less than 0.05 so it can be assumed that the interaction model is the more favourable model. 

##checking assumptions
```{r}
#| label: model_sqrt
#| tbl-cap: "Residual plots of square root model"
#plot of model
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model_sqrt)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Linearity: The Residuals vs Fitted plot of the model shows that points are symmetrically distributed along the horizontal line at zero, whilst some points are clustered in vertical stripes, most are positioned with reasonable variance, hence linearity can be reasonably assumed.

Normality: The points in the normal quantile plot show that the residuals lie mostly on a straight line with minimal divergence at either end, it can be assumed that the variables are normally distributed.

Homoscedasticity: The trend-line of the Scale-Location plot can be considered to be horizontal and points are not situated in a noticeable pattern although it also suggests an increase in spread so the assumption of homoscedasticity is not fully satisfied.

Independence: Independence of variables is difficult to determine as the procedures through which this data was collected is unknown. Polls from the same pollster or state may be related, pollsters may prefer a certain mode of polling, and 2012 has less than half of the number of polls (402) compared to 2016 (817), all of which may affect the assumption of independence. The lack of independence may affect standard errors and p-values. 

```{r}
#| label: vir-model_sqrt
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of variance inflation factors of predictor variables."
library(car)
car::vif(model_sqrt, type = 'predictor')
```

Using variance inflation factors and looking at GVIF\^(1/(2*Df) shows that all values fall below sqrt(5), while GVIF values for three of the four variables are above 5, looking at GVIF\^(1/(2*Df) is preferable, as to standardize for th differing degrees of freedom. The highest of these values is for days_to_election at 1.380. This indicates  multicollinearity may not be present between the variables.

```{r}
#| label: cooks-distance
#| tbl-cap: "Five largest cook's distance values."
head(sort(cooks.distance(model_sqrt), decreasing = TRUE), 5)

# Inspect the five largest Cook's distances for the square-root model
analysis[c(96, 7, 299, 219, 237),
         c("state", "year", "pollster", "mode", "absolute_error")]
```

All five largest cook's distance values are below the threshold value of 0.5. These observations remain in the data as there is no clear reason to remove them. All observations are from 2012 but from a variety of states, pollsters, and polling modes.

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of models with and without sensitivity check."
view(sensitivity_comparison) 
```

Comparing the coefficients of model without unususal values and those of the model with unsusual values, the greatest differences between coefficients are for year2016:modeIVR/Online (an increase of 0.0169), year2016 (an increase of 0.00510), year2016:modeInternet (a decrease of 0.00182), year2016:Undecided (an increse of 0.000640), and year2016:days_to_election (a decrease of 0.0000202). Four of these are coefficients from interaction terms.  The changes for the rest of the coefficients are magnitudes smaller. 

# Discussion

This investigation aimed to find whether polling error had any association with undecided voter share or polling method in the 2012 and/or 2016 US presidential elections, while also taking into account the days until the election. The overall conlcusion was that neither of these polling factors held a strong association with absolute polling error in the chosen fitted model. As indicated by the results, none of the predictors used appeared to have a statistically significant impact on polling error. This would suggest that neither undecided voter share nor polling method alone can explain differences in polling accuracy using the observation selected for this analysis.

In the model for the 2012 polls, the association between polling error and undecided voters was slightly positive however, in 2016, the interaction coefficient shows that the positive relationship is smaller. This indicates that there may be a difference in the association between undecided voters and polling error over different election periods. Nonetheless, the coefficients were still small, and the results did not find statistically significant evidence that the difference between years is meaningful. Hence, undecided voter share alone cannot be treated as a reliable predictor in this analysis.

Survey mode also differed slightly in its association with polling error between electoral periods. In 2012, IVR/Online and Internet polls had negative coefficients in relation to Live Phone polls. Yet in 2016, the interaction terms indicate that there was a change in the differences. The estimated Internet association with Live Phone changed to being positive, whereas the relationship between IVR/Online and Live Phone remained negative, indicating variance in the accuracy of polling methods between elections. However, it cannot be concluded that there is a statistically significant difference as the coefficients are measured on the sqaure root scale. Therefore, it cannot be determined for certain wherther there is a polling method that consistantly produced more accurate results.

## Limitations

The analysis performed identifies associations between predictors and response variables; this does not mean there is necessarily a causal relationship in the data. Other factors may also impact polling error. Polls with missing undecided voter shares were excluded, which may cause selection bias if such polls differ systematically from those that were included in the final dataset. In this investigation, only three survey modes were included; therefore, the associations found cannot be generalised to other survey modes. Polls from the same state and polling organisation could be related, which can affect the reliability of standard errors and confidence intervals, as the observations may not be independent. Finally, only two election periods were covered in this analysis, meaning that the findings may not be applicable to all elections, particularly historical elections that would not have used the same polling methods. It was also chosen to only analyse polls within a 90-day period of the election; it should be considered that associations may differ for polls outside of this period. The linear models created for this investigation are not highly accurate; other modelling methods could perform better. However, the focus of this investigation is linear modelling.

# Statistical appendix {#sec-appendix}

This appendix documents the data preparation, model comparison, diagnostics and sensitivity analysis. The analysis uses the cleaned polling data from the EDA and the election results in the project repository.

## Data preparation and sample selection {#sec-app-data}

The following code constructs the poll and election margins, identifies unusual reported totals and applies the sample selection rules. Missing response categories are ignored when calculating the reported total. The two unusual polls are excluded from `main_data` and retained in `sensitivity_data`.

```{r}
#| label: app-data-preparation
#| echo: true
#| results: hide
# Data preparation and sensitivity check

library(tidyverse)

# 1. Read the combined cleaned polling data and election results.
polls <- read_csv(
  "project datasets/clean/state_polls_combined_clean.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
elections <- read_csv(
  "project datasets/raw/1976-2024-president.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Check that each state-poll has a unique identifier.
sum(is.na(polls$poll_key)) # Count missing poll keys

sum(duplicated(polls$poll_key)) # Count duplicate poll keys

# 2. Count each major candidate's votes across all party labels.
# This includes votes reported on extra ballot lines, especially in New York.
elections <- elections |>
  filter(year %in% c(2012, 2016)) |>
  mutate(
    state = str_replace_all(str_to_lower(state), " ", "-"),
    state = if_else(state == "district-of-columbia", "washington-dc", state),
    candidate_group = case_when(
      year == 2012 & candidate == "OBAMA, BARACK H." ~ "Democrat",
      year == 2012 & candidate == "ROMNEY, MITT" ~ "Republican",
      year == 2016 & candidate == "CLINTON, HILLARY" ~ "Democrat",
      year == 2016 & candidate == "TRUMP, DONALD J." ~ "Republican",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

# Check Democrat and Republican records with no candidate name
unknown_candidate <- elections |>
  filter(
    is.na(candidate),
    party_simplified %in% c("DEMOCRAT", "REPUBLICAN")
  ) |>
  select(year, state, party_simplified, candidatevotes)

print(unknown_candidate)

# Each state-year should have one total-votes value.
vote_totals <- elections |>
  group_by(year, state) |>
  summarise(total_votes = first(totalvotes),
            number_of_totals = n_distinct(totalvotes), .groups = "drop")

# Count state-year records with different total-vote values
print(sum(vote_totals$number_of_totals != 1))

# Count state-year records with missing total votes
print(sum(is.na(vote_totals$total_votes)))

# Count state-year records with zero or negative total votes
print(sum(vote_totals$total_votes <= 0, na.rm = TRUE))

candidate_votes <- elections |>
  filter(!is.na(candidate_group)) |>
  group_by(year, state, candidate_group) |>
  summarise(votes = sum(candidatevotes), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = candidate_group, values_from = votes)

actual_results <- candidate_votes |>
  left_join(vote_totals, by = c("year", "state")) |>
  mutate(actual_margin = 100 * (Democrat - Republican) / total_votes) |>
  select(year, state, actual_margin)

# Count duplicate state-year election results
print(sum(duplicated(actual_results[c("year", "state")])))

# Count missing actual margins
print(sum(is.na(actual_results$actual_margin)))

# 3. Join each poll to its state-year election result.
polls <- polls |>
  left_join(actual_results, by = c("year", "state")) |>
  mutate(
    poll_margin = case_when(
      year == 2012 ~ Obama - Romney,
      year == 2016 ~ Clinton - Trump
    ),
    absolute_error = abs(poll_margin - actual_margin)
  )
# Count polls without a matching election result
print(sum(is.na(polls$actual_margin)))

# 4. Flag polls whose reported response percentages add to more than 102%.
# Missing categories are ignored when adding reported values.
# A high total may reflect rounding or reporting differences, so we do not indicate that it is an error.
polls <- polls |>
  mutate(
    reported_total = case_when(
      year == 2012 ~ rowSums(across(c(Obama, Romney, Undecided, Other)), na.rm = TRUE),
      year == 2016 ~ rowSums(across(c(Clinton, Trump, Undecided, Other, Johnson, McMullin)), na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    unusual_total = reported_total > 102
  )

# 5. Select polls from the final 90 days.
# Exclude polls with missing or non-positive sample size.
# After data exploration, we agree to include 3 modes: Live Phone, Internet and IVR/Online polls into the model. 
# Furthermore, we exclude the two flagged polls from the main sample
# and include them in a sensitivity check.

sample_90 <- polls |> filter(between(days_to_election, 0, 90))
valid <- sample_90 |>
  filter(!is.na(absolute_error), !is.na(sample_size), sample_size > 0)
# Polls that do not report undecided share are excluded; this may affect results.
complete <- valid |> filter(!is.na(Undecided))
selected <- complete |>
  filter(mode %in% c("Live Phone", "Internet", "IVR/Online")) |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(year, levels = c(2012, 2016)),
    mode = factor(mode, levels = c("Live Phone", "Internet", "IVR/Online"))
  )

main_data <- selected |> filter(!unusual_total)
sensitivity_data <- selected
unusual_records <- selected |>
  filter(unusual_total) |>
  select(poll_key, year, state, pollster, mode,
         Obama, Romney, Clinton, Trump, Undecided, Johnson, McMullin, Other,
         reported_total)

sample_counts <- tibble(
  stage = c("Cleaned polls", "Within 90 days", "Valid error and sample size",
            "Undecided reported", "Three modes", "Main sample"),
  remaining = c(nrow(polls), nrow(sample_90), nrow(valid), nrow(complete),
                nrow(selected), nrow(main_data))
) |>
  mutate(excluded_at_step = lag(remaining) - remaining)

print(sample_counts)
print(unusual_records, width = Inf)
print(table(main_data$year, main_data$mode))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sample-selection
#| tbl-cap: "Polls remaining after each selection step. The main analysis included 1,219 polls."
#| echo: true
knitr::kable(sample_counts)
```

## Model comparison and final model {#sec-app-model}

The additive and interaction models were fitted on the square-root scale. Their comparison tests the year interactions as a group. Reference groups are 2012 and Live Phone.

```{r}
#| label: app-fit-models
#| echo: true
# Fit the additive and interaction models to the same sample
model_sqrt_additive <- lm(
  sqrt(absolute_error) ~ Undecided + days_to_election + mode + year,
  data = main_data
)
model_sqrt <- lm(
  sqrt(absolute_error) ~ year * (Undecided + days_to_election + mode),
  data = main_data
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-app-model-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of additive and interaction models on the square-root scale. The F-test compares the year interactions as a group."
#| echo: true
knitr::kable(anova(model_sqrt_additive, model_sqrt), digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-model-detail
#| tbl-cap: "Final model coefficients and 95% confidence intervals on the square-root scale. The reference groups are 2012 and Live Phone."
#| echo: true
model_results <- cbind(Estimate = coef(model_sqrt), confint(model_sqrt))
knitr::kable(model_results, digits = 3)
```

## Diagnostic checks {#sec-app-checks}

The following plots examine residual patterns, normality, residual spread and influential observations.

```{r}
#| label: fig-diagnostics
#| fig-cap: "Diagnostic plots for the final square-root model. The Q-Q plot departs from the line at the tails, and the Scale-Location plot suggests a slight increase in residual spread."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7
#| echo: true
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model_sqrt)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-app-cooks
#| tbl-cap: "Five polls with the largest Cook's distances in the final model. The largest Cook's distance was approximately 0.014."
#| echo: true
# Inspect the polls with the largest Cook's distances
cook_values <- cooks.distance(model_sqrt)
top_polls <- head(order(cook_values, decreasing = TRUE), 5)
main_data |>
  slice(top_polls) |>
  select(poll_key, year, state, pollster, mode, absolute_error) |>
  mutate(Cooks_distance = cook_values[top_polls]) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

## Sensitivity analysis {#sec-app-sensitivity}

The same final model was refitted after adding the two unusual polls. Estimates are compared on the square-root scale.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-app-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity analysis on the square-root scale. Change is the estimate including the two unusual polls minus the main-sample estimate."
#| echo: true
model_with_unusual <- lm(
  sqrt(absolute_error) ~ year * (Undecided + days_to_election + mode),
  data = sensitivity_data
)

# Compare matching coefficient estimates
sensitivity_comparison <- tibble(
  Term = names(coef(model_sqrt)),
  Main_sample = unname(coef(model_sqrt)),
  With_unusual = unname(coef(model_with_unusual))
) |>
  mutate(Change = With_unusual - Main_sample)
knitr::kable(sensitivity_comparison, digits = 3)
```

The ordinary confidence intervals and F-test assume independent observations. Polls from the same state or pollster may be related, so these results should be interpreted with caution.
